title: Even Devadatta
hook: in the Lotus Sutra he too is promised Buddhahood, a Mahayana view (Lotus Sutra, Devadatta chapter)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devadatta's plots: hired men, a rock, an elephant, and a split. Your line was the split. Did you take one small step back across a line? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

What happens to Devadatta in the end? The Pali commentaries tell it starkly. Late in life, tradition says, he set out to see the Buddha and ask forgiveness, and the earth opened and swallowed him before he arrived. The same commentaries add a quieter line: that far in the future, even he will come to awakening. And in a Mahayana scripture, the Lotus Sutra, there's a chapter that carries his name and goes further still. It doesn't begin with Devadatta's crimes. It begins with a king, long ago, who wanted to learn. Today, even Devadatta.
screen: `THE EARTH OPENS.` → `A DOOR LEFT OPEN.` → `A CHAPTER WITH HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the king. In the chapter, the Buddha tells a story from one of his past lives. He was a king, he says, who wanted the highest teaching so much that he was ready to give up his throne for it. He announced that he would serve anyone who could teach him. Second, the seer. A seer came and said he knew a sutra, the Lotus, and would teach it if the king became his servant. So the king served him. He picked fruit, drew water, gathered firewood, prepared food, even let his own body be the seer's seat, and never wearied of it. Third, the name. Then the Buddha says who the seer was. That seer was Devadatta. And because of Devadatta, his good friend, the Buddha says, he came to complete the qualities of a buddha. Fourth, the promise. The chapter then says that after a vast stretch of time, Devadatta himself will become a buddha, named Heavenly King. This is a Mahayana view, and it's fair to say plainly whose it is. Theravada Buddhists read the Pali Vinaya and commentaries, where Devadatta's deeds bring heavy results, though the commentaries also leave that far door open. In some Mahayana schools, the Lotus chapter is read as saying that no one stands outside the reach of awakening, not even the cousin who rolled the rock. Some teachers also read it about enemies: the one who opposed you may turn out, in a long enough view, to be part of what formed you. Neither tradition says what Devadatta did was small. Both keep the warning. The Lotus chapter sets a promise beside it.
screen: `A KING WHO WANTED THE TEACHING.` · `A SEER WHO TAUGHT HIM.` · `THAT SEER WAS DEVADATTA.` · `HE TOO WILL BE A BUDDHA.` · then, large: `EVEN HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish one enemy well. Settle, and let the breath slow on its own. Bring to mind someone who has opposed you. Not the worst person you know. Someone in the middle: a rival, a critic, someone who made one season harder. If you practice loving-kindness, you might use the phrases that practice already uses, wishing them well and safe. If not, simply wish them one good thing: a good night's sleep, a kind word today. Wishing them well doesn't approve of anything they did. The Lotus chapter doesn't excuse Devadatta either. Just wish the one good thing, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Even Devadatta. In the Lotus Sutra, the cousin who split the sangha is named the Buddha's past teacher and promised buddhahood. Today's word.
Your line: even him. Today, when someone who has crossed you comes to mind, wish them one good thing before you move on. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: In some Mahayana communities the Lotus Sutra is chanted and studied, and its Devadatta chapter is read as a teaching that awakening reaches everyone; in Theravada communities Devadatta's story is told from the Pali Vinaya and commentaries as a warning about envy and ambition.

fork.setup: you're the king in the Buddha's story, and you want the highest teaching. a seer says he'll teach it, if you become his servant. what do you do?
options: refuse; a king serves no one.
serve him: fruit, water, firewood, whatever he needs.
send a servant in your place.
fork.reveal: the king serves him without wearying, and learns. then the Buddha reveals the seer was Devadatta.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the cousin's name, written in Devanagari.

trapdoor: what you thought: Devadatta is the villain, full stop.
what it means: in the Lotus Sutra's chapter he is also the seer who taught the Buddha in a past life, and he is promised buddhahood.
what a scholar hears: the promise is a Mahayana teaching; the Pali tradition keeps the harsher story, though its commentaries also foresee him awakening far in the future as a solitary buddha.
recall: foremost among nuns in psychic power

notes: The Devadatta chapter is a separate chapter (ch. 12) in Kumarajiva's Chinese version; in some Sanskrit versions the material sits within the Stupa chapter. The script cites only 'the Devadatta chapter', as the index does.
Confirm details of the king's service as paraphrased (fruit, water, firewood, food, his body as the seer's seat, never wearying) and the seer's name, Asita, omitted here.
Confirm the future buddha name 'Heavenly King' (Devaraja) and the phrase 'good friend' (kalyanamitra).

The Theravada account of Devadatta swallowed by the earth on his way to ask forgiveness, and his future awakening as the paccekabuddha Atthissara, is from the Dhammapada commentary (and Jataka commentary); confirm and confirm the fair phrasing 'leave that far door open'.
The reading about enemies ('part of what formed you') is attributed to 'some teachers'; confirm it is fair to Mahayana teaching on this chapter (e.g. Nichiren's reading).
The chapter's second episode, the naga king's daughter, is left out to keep one idea; consider for another day.
Editor pass: 'In Mahayana teaching' narrowed to 'some Mahayana schools'; closing contrast reworded so the Theravada reading is not framed as lacking (its commentaries also foresee his awakening).
